newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian jobless total climbs, no let-up in sight.
newsitem.headline: Italian jobless total climbs, no let-up in sight.

text.p: Italian unemployment, one of the biggest blots on the country's economic landscape, hit new highs in April as the labour market failed to absorb a growing workforce.
National statistics office Istat said Wednesday that unemployment rose to 12.5 percent in April. compared with 12.4 percent in January and 12.3 percent in April 1996.

The actual number of people looking for work grew by 59,000 to 2.88 million -- the highest level since new unemployment statistics were introduced in 1992. The situation was especially acute in the south of the country.
"We should now make a further effort to do everything possible to revive the economy," Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampihe told a banking conference after receiving the data.

Analysts, however, saw little chance of a swift recovery for the sluggish economy and said they expected Italy's jobless total, already well above the European Union average of 10.9 percent, to increase in the months ahead.

"We probably won't see a structural fall in unemployment until at least the middle of next year, when we hope to have a strengthening of the economic pick-up," said Pia Saraceno, director of the Institute for Social Research.
Istat said the total number of employed rose by 17,737 in April to 20.09 million, but this was not enough to absorb a 1.5 percent increase in the workforce.
Employment in the agriculture and industry sectors fell by 1.7 percent while the service sector saw a 1.1 percent rise.
"Overall we have a picture of stagnation. The number of people in work is basically the same but a larger number of people are now looking for a job," an Istat spokeswoman said.

The disparity between Italy's various regions remained marked, with a huge 22.5 percent of the workforce in the less developed south registered as unemployed against 10.7 percent in the nation's centre and 6.7 percent in the wealthy north.
The differences among the young was even wider, with some 56.1 percent of youths in the south jobless in April compared with 18.8 percent in the north.
However, the situation was not thought to be quite as severe as the statistics suggest with many people believed to have unregistered, cash-in-hand jobs.

"The unofficial unemployment rate has to be lower than stated in some parts of the country, otherwise you would have a revolution on your hands," Saraceno said. "It's clear society has found some sort of stability," she added.
